That is, the primary mirrors reads to each electable secondary at the specified sampling rate. Valid values are: `0.0`Turns off mirroring.`1.0`The primary mirrors all [operations that support mirroring](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/replication.md#std-label-mirrored-reads-supported-operations) to each electable secondary.Number between `0.0` and `1.0` (exclusive)The primary randomly samples each electable secondary at the specified rate to be sent mirrored reads. For example, given a replica set with a primary and two electable secondaries and a sampling rate of `0.10`, the primary mirrors reads to each electable secondary at the sampling rate of 10 percent such that one read may be mirrored to one secondary and not to the other or to both or to neither. That is, if the primary receives `100` operations that can be mirrored, the sampling rate of `0.10` may result in `8` reads being mirrored to one secondary and `13` reads to the other or `10` to each, etc. The default value is `0.01`. | | `maxTimeMS` | The maximum time in milliseconds for the mirrored reads. You can configure a node for targeted mirroring using the following syntax:`tag: { "<tag1>": "<string1>" }`You can only supply one tag. All nodes within the same replica set that have these tags are targeted.`samplingRate`*Type*: Float*Range*: `0.0` to `1.0` (inclusive)The rate at which targeted reads are mirrored to the host or hosts. ## How it works

- [passage] If you include a [`hint()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.hint.md#mongodb-method-cursor.hint) that specifies a [sparse index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#std-label-index-type-sparse) when you perform a [`count()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.count.md#mongodb-method-cursor.count) of all documents in a collection (i.e. with an empty query predicate), the sparse index is used even if the sparse index results in an incorrect count. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#sparse-index-and-incomplete-results · keywords: count, cursor, index, query shape, hint(), count()
- [passage] When you call [`count()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.count.md#mongodb-method-cursor.count) on a [`find()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.find.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.find) operation which does not specify a query predicate, the [`count()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.count.md#mongodb-method-cursor.count) method can return inaccurate document counts. These [`count()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.count.md#mongodb-method-cursor.count) methods return results based on the collection's metadata, which may result in an approximate count. In particular, — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.count.md#inaccurate-counts-without-query-predicate · keywords: count, cursor, query shape, count(), find()
- [passage] On a sharded cluster, [`count()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.count.md#mongodb-method-cursor.count) without a query predicate in the `find` can result in an *inaccurate* count if [orphaned documents](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-orphaned-document) exist or if a [chunk migration](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-balancer-administration.md#std-label-sharding-balancing) is in progress. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.count.md#sharded-clusters · keywords: count, cursor, query shape, count(), find · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/count.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.count.md

For an example, see [Perform Case-Insensitive Regular Expression Match.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/regex.md#std-label-regex-case-insensitive) | | `m` | For patterns that include anchors (`^` for the start, `$` for the end), match at the beginning or end of each line for strings with multiline values. Without this option, these anchors match at beginning or end of the string. For an example, see [Multiline Match for Lines Starting with Specified Pattern.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/regex.md#std-label-regex-multiline-match) If the pattern has no anchors or if the string value has no newline characters (for example, `\n`), the `m` option has no effect. | | `x` | "Extended" capability to ignore all white space characters in the `$regex` pattern unless escaped or included in a character class. Additionally, it ignores characters in-between and including an un-escaped hash/pound (`#`) character and the next new line, so that you may include comments in complicated patterns. This only applies to data characters; white space characters may never appear within special character sequences in a pattern. The `x` option does not affect the handling of the VT character (code 11). | | `s` | Allows the dot character (`.`) to match all characters *including* newline characters. For an example, see [Use the `.` Dot Character to Match New Line.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/regex.md#std-label-regex-dot-new-line) | | `u` | Unicode option, which is accepted but redundant. UTF is enabled by default for `$regex`. | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/regex.md#syntax · keywords: query operator anti-pattern,  | For patterns that include anchors (,  for the start, , \n,  option has no effect. | | , $regex

## How-to and procedures

- [passage] To check if MongoDB must perform an in-memory sort, append [`cursor.explain()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.explain.md#mongodb-method-cursor.explain) to the query and check the [explain results](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#std-label-explain-results). If the query plan contains a `SORT` stage, then MongoDB must perform an in-memory sort operation. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.sort.md#sort-and-index-use · keywords: blocking sort, cursor, index, cursor.explain(), SORT · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowDiskUse/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowDiskUse.md
- [passage] To include a regular expression in an `$in` query predicate operator, you can only use JavaScript regular expression objects (`/pattern/` ). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/regex.md#in-expressions · keywords: $in, query operator anti-pattern, query shape, /pattern/
- [passage] To determine whether a query is a covered query, use the [`db.collection.explain()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.explain.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.explain) or the [`explain()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.explain.md#mongodb-method-cursor.explain) method. See [Covered Queries.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#std-label-explain-output-covered-queries) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-optimization.md#explain-results · keywords: cursor, index, projection, db.collection.explain(), explain()
- [passage] To obtain the correct count of the number of documents in the `movies` collection, do not [`hint()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.hint.md#mongodb-method-cursor.hint) with a [sparse index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#std-label-index-type-sparse) when performing a count of all documents in a collection. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#sparse-index-and-incomplete-results · keywords: count, cursor, index, movies, hint()
- [passage] To avoid an in-memory sort, place the range filter after the sort predicate. ## Measurements and reference values

- [fact] The pseudo-random cursor walks the B-tree and is not guaranteed uniform; skew is likelier with unbalanced trees, many deleted documents, or many documents invisible to the transaction. For a uniform sample put another stage (such as $match) before $sample or use N above 5%, accepting the scan. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/sample/ · keywords: count, cursor, query operator anti-pattern, Count and Distinct and Sampling Optimization
- [statement] A community benchmark (July 2022) measured $or rising from 52 ms at 1,000 items to 11,684 ms at 20,000, while $in rose from 45 ms to 236 ms; the $or test had no index, so the comparison is unequal and is only directional evidence that $in scales better. — https://mongodb.com/community/forums/t/performance-of-or-vs-in/175513 · keywords: $in, index, query operator anti-pattern, $in and $or Index Bounds and Union Plans
- [passage] | Chart | Description | | --- | --- | | Connections | Number that indicates the total active connections to the cluster. Monitor connections to determine whether the current connection limits are sufficient. If necessary, scale the cluster tier. To learn more, see [Fix Connection Issues](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/connection-alerts.md#std-label-connection-alerts) and [Fix Lost Primary.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/no-primary.md#std-label-no-primary) Use [`$currentOp`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/currentOp.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-currentOp) to determine which collections are using more connections in a cluster. For more details, see [Count Collection Connections.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/currentOp/#count-collection-connections) | | Disk IOPS | Number that indicates the input operations per second. Monitor whether disk IOPS approaches the maximum provisioned IOPS. Determine whether the cluster can handle future workloads. To learn more, see [Fix IOPS Issues](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/disk-io-utilization.md#std-label-disk-io-util) and [Fix Lost Primary.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/no-primary.md#std-label-no-primary) | | Disk Usage | Number that indicates the total bytes of used disk space for the cluster. Monitor the combined size of your data and MongoDB operational data (buffer, journal, and log files) on the cluster. IMPORTANT: The UI displays GB, but all disk usage metrics are in gibibytes (GiB). To learn more, see [Fix Storage Issues.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/disk-space-used.md#std-label-disk-space-used) | | Query Targeting | Number that indicates the efficiency of read operations run on MongoDB. Monitor query targeting metrics to identify inefficient queries. The [change streams](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/changeStreams/) cursors that the MongoDB Search process (`mongot`) uses to keep MongoDB Search indexes updated can contribute to the query targeting ratio and trigger [query targeting alerts](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-conditions.md#std-label-query-targeting-alerts) if the ratio is high. To learn more, see [Fix Query Issues.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/query-targeting.md#std-label-query-targeting-resolution) | | Normalized System CPU | Number that indicates CPU usage of all processes on the node, scaled to a range of 0-100% by dividing by the number of CPU cores. Monitor CPU usage to determine whether to scale to a higher cluster tier. If you are unable to see the usage that triggered the alert, zoom in on the Normalized System CPU chart by clicking and dragging your mouse over the period of interest. With a higher-resolution view you may be able to identify acute spikes in CPU usage that weren't visible in the overview. To learn more, see [Fix IOPS Issues](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/disk-io-utilization.md#std-label-disk-io-util), [Fix Lost Primary](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/no-primary.md#std-label-no-primary), and [Fix CPU Usage Issues.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/system-cpu-usage.md#std-label-system-cpu) | | Oplog GB/Hour | Number that indicates the average rate in gigabytes of [oplog](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-oplog) data that the primary generates per hour. Monitor oplog data to determine whether you have to increase the oplog size. To learn more, see [Fix Oplog Issues.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/replication-oplog.md#std-label-replication-oplog-alerts) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/monitor-cluster-metrics.md#important-metrics · keywords: count, cursor, index, $currentOp, mongot
- [fact] $sample uses a pseudo-random cursor only if it is the first pipeline stage, N is under 5% of the collection (threshold not configurable), and the collection has more than 100 documents. Otherwise it reads all input and does a top-k random sort, which is subject to sort memory limits and can spill to disk. On a view $sample is never first, so it always scans. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/sample/ · keywords: count, cursor, Count and Distinct and Sampling Optimization
- [passage] If your use case requires a uniform sample, avoid the pseudo-random cursor. To do so, run $sample after another stage, or set N to more than 5% of the documents in the collection. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/sample/ · keywords: count, cursor
- [passage] If your use case requires a uniform sample, avoid the pseudo-random cursor. To do so, run [`$sample`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/sample.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-sample) after another stage, or set `N` to more than 5% of the documents in the collection. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/sample.md#pseudo-random-cursor-behavior · keywords: count, cursor, $sample
- [fact] allowDiskUse has no effect on sorts answered by an index, or on blocking sorts that fit under 100 MB. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowDiskUse/ · keywords: blocking sort, index, Blocking Sort and Index-Backed Sort
- [statement] A low-selectivity $nin on an indexed array field can be slower with the index than without it. In one forum report, the indexed plan examined about 3 million index keys and took about 1,962 ms; the COLLSCAN took about 107 ms. A document matches $nin only if none of its array keys match. The reporter forced a collection scan with hint({$natural:1}). Single anecdote, not a benchmark. — https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/index-is-slower-when-using-nin/112757 · keywords: index, query operator anti-pattern, Query Operator Anti-Patterns ($regex and negation and $where and $expr and $exists)
- [statement] Tencent Cloud reports that placing a range field ahead of the sort field forced an in-memory sort, and that reordering to ESR cut an order query from second-level latency to about 10 ms and a report from timeout to 200 ms. These are single-vendor anecdotes, not benchmarks. — https://intl.cloud.tencent.com/document/product/240/80772 · keywords: blocking sort, Blocking Sort and Index-Backed Sort
- [fact] Queries that involve multiple shards per request are less efficient and do not scale linearly when shards are added. A Netdata guide estimates a scatter-gather query on a 50-shard cluster can use up to 50x the CPU, memory and I/O of a targeted query. The 50x figure is an unbenchmarked estimate, not a measured number. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-choose-a-shard-key/ · keywords: sharded query targeting, Sharded Query Targeting and Scatter-Gather
- [passage] | **Instance RAM** | **Comparable Tier** | **maxIndexBuildMemoryUsageMegabytes Default** | | --- | --- | --- | | 256GB+ | M200+ | 2048 MB | | 128GB - 256GB | M80-M140 | 1024 MB | | 32GB - 128GB | M50-M60 | 512 MB | | 16GB | M40 | 400 MB | | 8GB | M30 | 250 MB | | 2GB - 4GB | M10-M20 | 100 MB | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#general-parameters · keywords: blocking sort
- [passage] `$changeStreamSplitLargeEvent` splits events that exceed 16 MB into fragments and returns the fragments sequentially using the change stream cursor. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/changeStreamSplitLargeEvent.md#behavior · keywords: cursor, $changeStreamSplitLargeEvent
- [fact] estimatedDocumentCount() can be inaccurate after an unclean shutdown (drift depends on writes since the last checkpoint, usually 60 s) and on a sharded cluster does not filter orphaned documents; running validate on each collection restores the count statistic. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.estimatedDocumentCount/ · keywords: count, Count and Distinct and Sampling Optimization

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [passage] | **MongoDB Version** | **Changes** | | --- | --- | | 6.1 | Slow operation log messages include [cache refresh time fields.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#std-label-log-messages-cache-refresh-times) | | 6.2 | Slow operation log messages include a `queryFramework` field that indicates which query engine executed the query: `queryFramework: "classic"` indicates that the classic engine executed the query.; `queryFramework: "sbe"` indicates that the slot-based query execution engine executed the query. | | 6.3 | Slow operation log messages and [database profiler](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md#std-label-profiler) entries include a `cpuNanos` field that specifies the total CPU time spent by a query operation in nanoseconds. The `cpuNanos` field is only available on Linux systems. | | 7.0 (and 6.0.13, 5.0.24) | The `totalOplogSlotDurationMicros` in the slow query log message shows the time between a write operation getting a commit timestamp to commit the storage engine writes and actually committing. `mongod` supports parallel writes. However, it commits write operations with commit timestamps in any order. For example, consider the following writes with commit timestamps: writeA with Timestamp1; writeB with Timestamp2; writeC with Timestamp3 Suppose writeB commits first at Timestamp2. Replication is paused until writeA commits because writeA's oplog entry with Timestamp1 is required for replication to copy the oplog to secondary replica set members. | | 8.0 | The slow query output includes a `queues` document that contains information about the operation's [queues](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/serverstatus.md#std-label-server-status-queues). Each queue in the `queues` field contains a `totalTimeQueuedMicros` field that contains the total cumulative time in microseconds that the operation spent in the corresponding queue. The `queryShapeHash` field for a [query shape](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-shapes.md#std-label-query-shapes) is also included in the slow query log when available. If a command with a specific query shape is [rejected](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/operation-rejection-filters.md#std-label-operation-rejection-filters), MongoDB logs a message that states the query command was rejected. The message contains the query namespace, `queryShapeHash`, and the command with the rejected query. MongoDB only logs the message if the log verbosity level is set to at least `2`. | | 8.1 | Slow query log messages contain new metrics if the query execution writes temporary files to disk. These metrics are prefixed by the query execution stage that caused the query to exceed the memory limit. For example, `sortSpills` indicates the number of times that the sort stage of query execution wrote temporary files to disk. `<executionPart>Spills` indicates the number of times the corresponding query execution stage wrote temporary files to disk.; `<executionPart>SpilledBytes` indicates the size, in bytes, of the memory released by writing temporary files to disk.; `<executionPart>SpilledDataStorageSize` indicates the size, in bytes, of disk space used for temporary files.; `<executionPart>SpilledRecords` indicates the number of records written to temporary files on disk. For more information on writing temporary files to disk, see [`allowDiskUse()`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowdiskuse.md#mongodb-method-cursor.allowDiskUse) | | 8.3 | Slow query log entries have an optional `originalQueryShapeHash` field that contains that query shape of the following operations that originate on the [`mongos`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongos.md#std-program-mongos) : [`find`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.find); [`aggregate`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/aggregate.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.aggregate); [`count`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/count.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.count); [`distinct`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/distinct.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.distinct) The original query shape of the `mongos` operation may differ after the `mongos` sends the operation to the [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#std-program-mongod) . MongoDB 8.3 also introduces slow in-progress query log entries. Queries trigger a slow-in progress log during execution. These logs contain less information than standard slow query logs. MongoDB logs queries at most once if the query's duration surpasses the [`operationProfiling.slowOpInProgressThresholdMs`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/configuration-options.md#mongodb-setting-operationProfiling.slowOpInProgressThresholdMs) When an operation specifies a [time limit for a query](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/query-documents/specify-query-timeout.md#std-label-manual-query-timeout), slow query logs contain a `deadline` field. `deadline` indicates the time the operation must complete by, which is equal to the time at the start of the operation plus the value of the query timeout. | | 9.0 | When a query shape has query knobs set through [`setQuerySettings`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setquerysettings.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.setQuerySettings) or [`setParameter`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setparameter.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.setParameter), slow query log entries include a `queryKnobs` document. The document shows the effective value of each knob and where the value comes from, with the same shape as the [explain output](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#std-label-explain-output-query-knobs). For details, see [Query Knobs.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setquerysettings.md#std-label-setQuerySettings-query-knobs) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#version-specific-changes · keywords: blocking sort, count, cursor, index, query shape, sharded query targeting
- [fact] Sort and limit behave differently in the router. Unsorted results come from a round-robin over shard cursors. With limit(), mongos passes the limit to each shard and re-applies it to the merged result. With skip(), mongos cannot push the skip down: it passes limit+skip to the shards, then skips while assembling results. Deep skip on a sharded collection therefore costs more. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharded-cluster-query-router/ · keywords: blocking sort, cursor, pagination, sharded query targeting, Sharded Query Targeting and Scatter-Gather
- [fact] ESR classification: $ne, $nin and $regex are range operators, not equality. $in alone is equality. With a sort, $in under 201 elements expands and merges via a SORT_MERGE stage (acts like equality); at 201 or more it behaves like a range and later index keys cannot supply the sort. The 201 threshold is documented as not guaranteed across versions. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline/ · keywords: $in, blocking sort, index, query operator anti-pattern, Blocking Sort and Index-Backed Sort

- [passage] | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `count` | string | The name of the collection or view to count. | | `query` | document | Optional. A query that selects which documents to count in the collection or view. | | `limit` | integer | Optional. The maximum number of matching documents to return. | | `skip` | integer | Optional. The number of matching documents to skip before returning results. | | `hint` | string or document | Optional. The index to use. Specify either the index name as a string or the index specification document. | | `readConcern` | document | Optional. Specifies the [read concern](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-read-concern). The option has the following syntax: `readConcern: { level: <value> }` Possible read concern levels are: [`"local"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-local.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-local-). This is the default read concern level for read operations against the primary and secondaries.; [`"available"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-available.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-available-). Available for read operations against the primary and secondaries. [`"available"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-available.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-available-) behaves the same as [`"local"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-local.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-local-) against the primary and non-sharded secondaries. The query returns the instance's most recent data.; [`"majority"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-majority.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-majority-). Available for replica sets that use [WiredTiger storage engine.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/wiredtiger.md#std-label-storage-wiredtiger); [`"linearizable"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-linearizable.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-linearizable-). Available for read operations on the [`primary`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/replica-states.md#mongodb-replstate-replstate.PRIMARY) only.; [`"snapshot"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-snapshot.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-snapshot-). Available for [multi-document transactions](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/transactions.md#std-label-transactions) and certain read operations outside of multi-document transactions. For more formation on the read concern levels, see [Read Concern Levels.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern.md#std-label-read-concern-levels) | | `maxTimeMS` | non-negative integer | Optional. Specifies a time limit in milliseconds. If you do not specify a value for `maxTimeMS`, operations will not time out. A value of `0` explicitly specifies the default unbounded behavior. MongoDB terminates operations that exceed their allotted time limit using the same mechanism as [`db.killOp()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.killop.md#mongodb-method-db.killOp). MongoDB only terminates an operation at one of its designated [interrupt points.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-interrupt-point) | | `collation` | document | Optional. Optional. Specifies the [collation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation) to use for the operation. [Collation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation) allows users to specify language-specific rules for string comparison, such as rules for lettercase and accent marks. The collation option has the following syntax: `collation: { locale: <string>, caseLevel: <boolean>, caseFirst: <string>, strength: <int>, numericOrdering: <boolean>, alternate: <string>, maxVariable: <string>, backwards: <boolean> }` When specifying collation, the `locale` field is mandatory; all other collation fields are optional. For descriptions of the fields, see [Collation Document.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation-document-fields) If the collation is unspecified but the collection has a default collation (see [`db.createCollection()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.createcollection.md#mongodb-method-db.createCollection)), the operation uses the collation specified for the collection. If no collation is specified for the collection or for the operations, MongoDB uses the simple binary comparison used in prior versions for string comparisons. You cannot specify multiple collations for an operation. For example, you cannot specify different collations per field, or if performing a find with a sort, you cannot use one collation for the find and another for the sort. | | `comment` | any | Optional. - [fact] To detect a broadcast: run explain('executionStats') through mongos and check whether the shards array lists every shard or the top stage is SHARD_MERGE. - [passage] If MongoDB cannot obtain the sort order with an index scan, then MongoDB uses a top-k sort algorithm. This algorithm buffers the first `k` results (or last, depending on the sort order) seen so far by the underlying index or collection access. If the memory footprint of these `k` results exceeds 100 megabytes, MongoDB automatically writes temporary files to disk unless the query specifies [`cursor.allowDiskUse()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowdiskuse.md#mongodb-method-cursor.allowDiskUse) with a value of `false` (in which case, the query fails). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.sort.md#limit-results · keywords: blocking sort, cursor, index, cursor.allowDiskUse(), false
- [passage] Since reading.timestamp is not included in an index, MongoDB must perform an in-memory sort operation to return results in the requested sort order. By specifying cursor.allowDiskUse(false), MongoDB cannot process the sort operation if it requires more than 100 megabytes of system memory. If the operation requires more than 100 megabytes of system memory, MongoDB would return an error. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowDiskUse/ · keywords: blocking sort, cursor, index · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowDiskUse.md
- [fact] ESR guideline: $in used alone is an equality operator (a series of equality matches). With .sort(), an $in of fewer than 201 elements is expanded and merged in index sort order by a SORT_MERGE stage, behaving like equality; with 201 or more elements it is ordered like a range, subsequent index fields cannot be used for sorting, and it behaves like a range predicate. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline/ · keywords: $in, blocking sort, index, $in and $or Index Bounds and Union Plans

WARNING: If the [`ShardingTaskExecutorPoolReplicaSetMatching`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.ShardingTaskExecutorPoolReplicaSetMatching) is set to `"automatic"`, the [`replicaSetMatchingStrategy`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/connpoolstats.md#mongodb-data-connPoolStats.replicaSetMatchingStrategy) still describes the actual policy being used, not `"automatic"`. To find the value of the [`ShardingTaskExecutorPoolReplicaSetMatching`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.ShardingTaskExecutorPoolReplicaSetMatching), use [`getParameter`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/getparameter.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.getParameter) which returns the value of the server parameter. | | `"matchPrimaryNode"` | When set for a [`mongos`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongos.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongos), the minimum size limit of the instance's connection pool to each secondary of a replica set in the sharded cluster (specifically, shard replica set and config servers) is equal to the size of its connection pool to that replica set's primary. When set for a [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongod), the minimum size limit of the instance's connection pool to each secondary of another replica set in the sharded cluster (specifically, shard replica set and config servers) is equal to the size of its connection pool to that replica set's primary. WARNING: If multiple shard servers in your topology can experience a rapid influx of cross-shard operations, do not set this option on your [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongod) instances. In case of a primary stepdown, `matchPrimaryNode` ensures that any secondary that becomes the primary can handle the current level of primary reads and writes. | | `"matchBusiestNode"` | When set for a [`mongos`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongos.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongos), the instance's minimum size limit of the connection pool to each member of a replica set in the sharded cluster (specifically, shard replica set and config servers) is equal to the largest among the active connection counts to the primary and each secondary member of that replica set. When set for a [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongod), the instance's minimum size limit of the connection pool to each member of another replica set in the sharded cluster (specifically, shard replica set and config servers) is equal to the largest among the active connection counts to the primary and each secondary member of that replica set. With `"matchBusiestNode"`, [`mongos`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongos.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongos) maintains enough connections to each secondary to handle the current level of primary and secondary reads and writes. The number of connections to maintain in the pool decreases as the number of active connections decreases. | | `"disabled"` | When set for a [`mongos`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongos.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongos), the instance's minimum number of connections in the instance's connection pool to each node of a replica set in the sharded clusterv (specifically, shard replica set and config servers) is equal to the [`ShardingTaskExecutorPoolMinSize`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.ShardingTaskExecutorPoolMinSize) When set for a [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongod), the instance's minimum number of connections in the instance's connection pool to each node of another replica set in the sharded cluster (specifically, shard replica set and config servers) is equal to the [`ShardingTaskExecutorPoolMinSize`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.ShardingTaskExecutorPoolMinSize) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#sharding-parameters · keywords: count, read preference, sharded query targeting, "automatic", mongos, "matchPrimaryNode"

For example: Consider the following wildcard projection document: `{ "product_attributes.elements" : 1, "product_attributes.resistance" : 1 }` If your index field name is `$**`, your index only includes the values of the fields in that projection. | [Create a Wildcard Index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/indexes.md#std-label-atlas-ui-wildcard-index) | | Use custom collation | Create a custom collation for the index by typing or pasting the collation document in the text box. | [Collation Document](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation/#collation-document) | | Create sparse index | Index skips over any document that is missing the indexed field. | [Sparse Indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#std-label-index-type-sparse) | | Build in rolling process | Can minimize the performance impact of index builds. IMPORTANT: Building an index in a rolling fashion reduces the resiliency of your cluster and increases index build times. We only recommend using rolling index builds when regular index builds do not meet your needs. WARNING: Avoid performing rolling index and replicated index build processes concurrently as it might lead to unexpected issues, such as broken builds and crash loops. You can only build rolling indexes on M10+ Clusters. During a rolling index build, Atlas takes each node out of the replica set, starts it in standalone mode to build the index, and then returns it to the replica set. This process repeats for each node in the cluster in a rolling sequence. Nodes may appear as down, while Atlas builds indexes offline. This is expected behavior, not an issue. | [Rolling Index Builds](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/rolling-index-builds.md#std-label-rolling-index-build) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/indexes.md#create-an-index · keywords: index, projection, query operator anti-pattern, unique, timezone, { "timezone": { "$exists": true } }

- [fact] distinct operations can use indexes and can be covered by them. For array fields distinct treats each array element as a separate value. On sharded clusters distinct may return orphaned documents; on time series collections it cannot use indexes efficiently and the docs say to use $group; in transactions on sharded collections distinct is not allowed and $group must be used. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/distinct/ · keywords: count, index, Count and Distinct and Sampling Optimization
- [statement] Very large $or lists were slow in the planner because IndexBoundsBuilder::unionize() merged clause bounds one at a time (roughly quadratic); SERVER-34012 was fixed in 5.0.0-rc0. The reporter's diagnostic patch cut a 20,000-clause query from ~40 s to ~400 ms; the official fix's gain is not stated. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-34012 · keywords: $in, index, $in and $or Index Bounds and Union Plans
- [fact] Not every index type can cover queries; hashed indexes cannot be multikey, and support must be checked on each index type's docs page. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-optimization/ · keywords: index, projection, Projection Optimization and Covered Query Design

- [fact] Case-insensitive indexes (collation) do not help $regex, because $regex is not collation-aware. The case-insensitive (i) option therefore forfeits efficient prefix bounds. - [fact] $where evaluates JavaScript for each document and cannot take advantage of indexes. Alone it requires a collection scan. MongoDB evaluates the non-$where predicates first, and those can use an index, so always pair $where with at least one indexable standard predicate. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/where.md · keywords: index, query operator anti-pattern, Query Operator Anti-Patterns ($regex and negation and $where and $expr and $exists)

Default: 100 The slow operation time threshold, in milliseconds. Operations that run for longer than this threshold are considered *slow*. Slow operations are logged based on `workingMillis`, which is the amount of time that MongoDB spends working on that operation. This means that factors such as waiting for locks and flow control do not affect whether an operation exceeds the slow operation threshold. When [`logLevel`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.logLevel) is set to `0`, MongoDB records *slow* operations to the diagnostic log at a rate determined by [`slowOpSampleRate`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/configuration-options.md#mongodb-setting-operationProfiling.slowOpSampleRate) At higher `logLevel` settings, all operations appear in the diagnostic log regardless of their latency with the following exception: the logging of slow oplog entry messages by the secondaries. The secondaries log only the slow oplog entries; increasing the `logLevel` does not log all oplog entries. This argument affects the same setting as the configuration option [`operationProfiling.slowOpThresholdMs`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/configuration-options.md#mongodb-setting-operationProfiling.slowOpThresholdMs) | | `sampleRate` | double | Optional. Default: 1.0 The fraction of *slow* operations that should be profiled or logged. `sampleRate` accepts values between 0 and 1, inclusive. This argument affects the same setting as the configuration option [`operationProfiling.slowOpSampleRate`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/configuration-options.md#mongodb-setting-operationProfiling.slowOpSampleRate) and does not affect the slow oplog entry log messages on secondaries. | | `filter` | object | Optional. When set, the `batchSize` is the lesser of `batchSize` documents or 16 MiB worth of documents. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.batchSize.md#definition · keywords: cursor, 101, batchSize · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/queryStats/

When using the regex `/<pattern>/`, you can also specify the regex options `i` and `m` (but not the `s` or `x` options): `"pattern"`; `/<pattern>/`; `/<pattern>/<options>` Alternatively, you can also specify the regex options with the [options](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/regexmatch.md#std-label-regexMatch-options) field. To specify the `s` or `x` options, you must use the [options](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/regexmatch.md#std-label-regexMatch-options) field. You cannot specify options in both the `regex` and the `options` field. | | [options](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/regexmatch.md#std-label-regexMatch-options) | *Optional*. The following `<options>` are available for use with regular expression. You cannot specify options in both the `regex` and the `options` field. `i`: Case insensitivity to match both upper and lower cases. You can specify the option in the `options` field or as part of the regex field.; `m`: For patterns that include anchors (that is, `^` for the start, `$` for the end), match at the beginning or end of each line for strings with multiline values. Without this option, these anchors match at beginning or end of the string.If the pattern contains no anchors or if the string value has no newline characters (e.g. `\n`), the `m` option has no effect.; `x`: "Extended" capability to ignore all white space characters in the pattern unless escaped or included in a character class.Additionally, it ignores characters in-between and including an un-escaped hash/pound (`#`) character and the next new line, so that you may include comments in complicated patterns. This only applies to data characters; white space characters may never appear within special character sequences in a pattern.The `x` option does not affect the handling of the VT character (code 11).You can specify the option only in the `options` field.; `s`: Allows the dot character (`.`) to match all characters *including* newline characters.You can specify the option only in the `options` field. | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/regexMatch.md#syntax · keywords: query operator anti-pattern, /<pattern>/,  and ,  (but not the ,  or ,  options):  · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/regexFindAll.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/regexFind.md

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [passage] | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `find` | string | The name of the collection or [view](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/views.md#std-label-views-landing-page) to query. | | `filter` | document | Optional. The query predicate. If unspecified, all documents in the collection match the predicate. | | [sort](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#std-label-find-cmd-sort) | document | Optional. The sort specification for the ordering of the results. | | `projection` | document | Optional. The [projection specification](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/project-fields-from-query-results.md#std-label-projections) to determine which fields to include in the returned documents. [`find()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.find.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.find) operations on views do not support the following [find command projection operators:](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/mql/projection.md#std-label-projection-operators-ref) [`$`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/projection/positional.md#mongodb-projection-proj.-); [`$elemMatch`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/projection/elemmatch.md#mongodb-projection-proj.-elemMatch); [`$slice`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/projection/slice.md#mongodb-projection-proj.-slice); [`$meta`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/meta.md#mongodb-expression-exp.-meta) | | `hint` | string or document | Optional. Index specification. Specify either the index name as a string or the index key pattern. If specified, the query system only considers plans using the hinted index. With the following exception, `hint` is required if the command includes the `min` or `max` fields. `hint` is not required with `min` or `max` if the `filter` is an equality condition on the `_id` field `{ _id: <value> }`. | | `skip` | positive integer | Optional. Number of documents to skip. Defaults to 0. | | `limit` | non-negative integer | Optional. The maximum number of documents to return. If unspecified, then defaults to no limit. A limit of 0 is equivalent to setting no limit. | | `batchSize` | non-negative integer | Optional. The maximum number of documents that can be returned in each batch of a query result. By default, the `find` command has an initial `batchSize` of the lesser of `101` documents or 16 mebibytes (MiB) worth of documents. Subsequent batches have a maximum size of 16 MiB. This option can enforce a smaller limit than 16 MiB, but not a larger one. When set, the `batchSize` is the lesser of `batchSize` documents or 16 MiB worth of documents. A `batchSize` of `0` means that the cursor is established, but no documents are returned in the first batch. Unlike the previous wire protocol version, a batchSize of 1 for the [`find`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.find) command does not close the cursor. To specify batch size for subsequent [`getMore`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/getmore.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.getMore) operations, use [`batchSize()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.batchsize.md#mongodb-method-cursor.batchSize) in mongosh. | | `singleBatch` | boolean | Optional. Determines whether to close the cursor after the first batch. Defaults to false. | | `comment` | any | Optional. A user-provided comment to attach to this command. Once set, this comment appears alongside records of this command in the following locations: [mongod log messages](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#std-label-log-messages-ref), in the `attr.command.cursor.comment` field.; [Database profiler](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md#std-label-profiler) output, in the [`command.comment`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md#mongodb-data-system.profile.command) field.; [`currentOp`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/currentop.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.currentOp) output, in the [`command.comment`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/currentop.md#mongodb-data-currentOp.command) field. A comment can be any valid [BSON type](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/bson-types.md#std-label-bson-types) (string, integer, object, array, etc). Any comment set on a `find` command is inherited by any subsequent [`getMore`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/getmore.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.getMore) commands run on the `find` cursor. | | `maxTimeMS` | non-negative integer | Optional. Specifies a time limit in milliseconds. If you do not specify a value for `maxTimeMS`, operations will not time out. A value of `0` explicitly specifies the default unbounded behavior. MongoDB terminates operations that exceed their allotted time limit using the same mechanism as [`db.killOp()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.killop.md#mongodb-method-db.killOp). MongoDB only terminates an operation at one of its designated [interrupt points.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-interrupt-point) When specifying [`linearizable read concern`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-linearizable.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-linearizable-), always use `maxTimeMS` in case a majority of data bearing members are unavailable. `maxTimeMS` ensures that the operation does not block indefinitely and instead returns an error if the read concern cannot be fulfilled. [`maxTimeMS()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.maxtimems.md#mongodb-method-cursor.maxTimeMS) is unrelated to [`noCursorTimeout()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.nocursortimeout.md#mongodb-method-cursor.noCursorTimeout). [`maxTimeMS()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.maxtimems.md#mongodb-method-cursor.maxTimeMS) limits processing time, while [`noCursorTimeout()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.nocursortimeout.md#mongodb-method-cursor.noCursorTimeout) prevents idle-time expiration. A cursor's idle time does not contribute to its processing time. | | `readConcern` | document | Optional. Specifies the [read concern.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-read-concern) The `readConcern` option has the following syntax: `readConcern: { level: <value> }` Possible read concern levels are: [`"local"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-local.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-local-). This is the default read concern level for read operations against the primary and secondaries.; [`"available"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-available.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-available-). Available for read operations against the primary and secondaries. [`"available"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-available.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-available-) behaves the same as [`"local"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-local.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-local-) against the primary and non-sharded secondaries. The query returns the instance's most recent data.; [`"majority"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-majority.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-majority-). Available for replica sets that use [WiredTiger storage engine.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/wiredtiger.md#std-label-storage-wiredtiger); [`"linearizable"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-linearizable.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-linearizable-). Available for read operations on the [`primary`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/replica-states.md#mongodb-replstate-replstate.PRIMARY) only.; [`"snapshot"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-snapshot.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-snapshot-). Available for [multi-document transactions](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/transactions.md#std-label-transactions) and certain read operations outside of multi-document transactions. For more formation on the read concern levels, see [Read Concern Levels.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern.md#std-label-read-concern-levels) The [`getMore`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/getmore.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.getMore) command uses the `readConcern` level specified in the originating `find` command. | | `max` | document | Optional. The *exclusive* upper bound for a specific index. See [`cursor.max()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.max.md#mongodb-method-cursor.max) for details. To use the `max` field, the command must also use `hint` unless the specified `filter` is an equality condition on the `_id` field `{ _id: <value> }`. | | `min` | document | Optional. The *inclusive* lower bound for a specific index. See [`cursor.min()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.min.md#mongodb-method-cursor.min) for details. To use the `min` field, the command must also use `hint` unless the specified `filter` is an equality condition on the `_id` field `{ _id: <value> }`. | | `returnKey` | boolean | Optional. If true, returns only the index keys in the resulting documents. Defaults to false. If returnKey is true and the [`find`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.find) command does not use an index, the returned documents are empty. | | `showRecordId` | boolean | Optional. Determines whether to return the record identifier for each document. If true, adds a field $recordId to the returned documents. | | `tailable` | boolean | Optional. Returns a [tailable cursor](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-tailable-cursor) for a capped collections. | | `awaitData` | boolean | Optional. Use with the tailable option to block a [`getMore`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/getmore.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.getMore) command on the cursor temporarily at the end of data rather than returning no data. After a timeout period, [`find`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.find) returns as normal. | | `noCursorTimeout` | boolean | Optional. Prevents the server from timing out non-session idle cursors after an inactivity period of 30 minutes. Ignored for cursors that are part of a session. For more information, see [Session Idle Timeout.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#std-label-session-idle-timeout) | | [allowPartialResults](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#std-label-cmd-find-allowPartialResults) | boolean | Optional. For queries against a sharded collection, allows the command (or subsequent [`getMore`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/getmore.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.getMore) commands) to return partial results instead of an error if one or more queried shards are unavailable. If [`find`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.find) (or subsequent [`getMore`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/getmore.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.getMore) commands) returns partial results because the queried shard(s) aren't available, the [find output](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#std-label-cmd-find-output) includes a `partialResultsReturned` indicator field. If the queried shards are available for the initial `find` command, but one or more shards become unavailable for subsequent `getMore` commands, only the `getMore` commands that run while the shards aren't available include `partialResultsReturned` in their output. | | `collation` | document | Optional. Optional. Specifies the [collation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation) to use for the operation. [Collation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation) allows users to specify language-specific rules for string comparison, such as rules for lettercase and accent marks. The collation option has the following syntax: `collation: { locale: <string>, caseLevel: <boolean>, caseFirst: <string>, strength: <int>, numericOrdering: <boolean>, alternate: <string>, maxVariable: <string>, backwards: <boolean> }` When specifying collation, the `locale` field is mandatory; all other collation fields are optional. For descriptions of the fields, see [Collation Document.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation-document-fields) If the collation is unspecified but the collection has a default collation (see [`db.createCollection()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.createcollection.md#mongodb-method-db.createCollection)), the operation uses the collation specified for the collection. If no collation is specified for the collection or for the operations, MongoDB uses the simple binary comparison used in prior versions for string comparisons. You cannot specify multiple collations for an operation. For example, you cannot specify different collations per field, or if performing a find with a sort, you cannot use one collation for the find and another for the sort. | | [allowDiskUse](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#std-label-find-cmd-allowDiskUse) | boolean | Optional. Use this option to override [`allowDiskUseByDefault`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.allowDiskUseByDefault) for a specific query. You can use this option to either: Prohibit disk use on a system where disk use is allowed by default.; Allow disk use on a system where disk use is prohibited by default. Starting in MongoDB 6.0, if [`allowDiskUseByDefault`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.allowDiskUseByDefault) is set to `true` and the server requires more than 100 megabytes of memory for a pipeline execution stage, MongoDB automatically writes temporary files to disk unless the query specifies `{ allowDiskUse: false }`. For details, see [`allowDiskUseByDefault`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.allowDiskUseByDefault) `allowDiskUse` has no effect if MongoDB can satisfy the specified [sort](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#std-label-find-cmd-sort) using an index, *or* if the in-memory sort requires less than 100 megabytes of memory. For more complete documentation on `allowDiskUse`, see [`cursor.allowDiskUse()`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowdiskuse.md#mongodb-method-cursor.allowDiskUse) For more information on memory restrictions for large in-memory sorts, see [Sort and Index Use.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.sort.md#std-label-sort-index-use) | | [let](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#std-label-find-let-syntax) | document | Optional. Specifies a document with a list of variables. This allows you to improve command readability by separating the variables from the query text. The document syntax is: `{ <variable_name_1>: <expression_1>, ..., <variable_name_n>: <expression_n> }` The variable is set to the value returned by the expression, and cannot be changed afterwards. To access the value of a variable in the command, use the double dollar sign prefix (`$$`) together with your variable name in the form `$$<variable_name>`. For example: `$$targetTotal`. To use a variable to filter results, you must access the variable within the [`$expr`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/expr.md#mongodb-query-op.-expr) operator. For a complete example using `let` and variables, see [Use Variables in `let`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#std-label-find-let-example) **New in version 5.0** | | `querySettings` | document | Optional. Query settings that apply only to this execution of the command. The `querySettings` document accepts the following fields: `indexHints`; `queryFramework`; `reject`; `comment`; `queryKnobs`; `maxTimeMS` For descriptions of these fields, see [Command Fields.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setquerysettings.md#std-label-setQuerySettings-fields) MongoDB doesn't store these settings on the cluster, and they don't apply to other queries with the same [query shape](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-shapes.md#std-label-query-shapes). To set query settings that persist for a query shape, use [`setQuerySettings`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setquerysettings.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.setQuerySettings) MongoDB combines the settings that you pass in the command with any query settings stored on the cluster for the same query shape. If both settings specify the same field, the stored cluster setting takes precedence. **New in version 9.0** | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#command-fields · keywords: blocking sort, cursor, index, projection, query operator anti-pattern, query shape
- [passage] | Option | Description | | --- | --- | | allowDiskUse | Whether or not pipelines that require more than 100 megabytes of memory to execute write to temporary files on disk. For details, see [`cursor.allowDiskUse()`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowdiskuse.md#mongodb-method-cursor.allowDiskUse) | | allowPartialResults | For queries against a sharded collection, allows the command (or subsequent getMore commands) to return partial results, rather than an error, if one or more queried shards are unavailable. | | awaitData | If the cursor is a a tailable-await cursor. When sorting on a field which contains duplicate values, documents containing those values may be returned in any order. The `$sort` operation is not a "stable sort," which means that documents with equivalent sort keys are not guaranteed to remain in the same relative order in the output as they were in the input. If the field specified in the sort criteria does not exist in two documents, then the value on which they are sorted is the same. The two documents may be returned in any order. - [fact] On a sharded cluster each shard samples independently and mongos samples the merged result. SERVER-68623 (closed Won't Do, 2022-09-28) reports each shard gets the full requested size and so picks random sort instead of the cursor, because a mongod does not know the cluster-wide document count; the 5% rule is documented only for mongod behaviour. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/sample/ · keywords: count, cursor, sharded query targeting, Count and Distinct and Sampling Optimization
- [fact] Adding an array field to a compound index to 'complete' coverage can backfire: in a forum case the index became multikey, the plan fell back to PROJECTION_SIMPLE (not covered), and the poster measured 100 s vs 6 s versus the index without the array field (5.1M docs, MongoDB 4.0.10). — https://mongodb.com/community/forums/t/adding-the-projected-fields-to-compound-index-to-create-covered-query-doesnt-improve-performance/199267 · keywords: index, projection, query operator anti-pattern, Projection Optimization and Covered Query Design

If this index is the last remaining shard key index, `dropIndexes` raises an error.; To drop multiple indexes, specify an array of the index names. | | writeConcern | document | Optional. A document expressing the [write concern](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/write-concern.md) of the [`drop`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/drop.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.drop) command. Omit to use the default write concern. | | `comment` | any | Optional. A user-provided comment to attach to this command. Once set, this comment appears alongside records of this command in the following locations: [mongod log messages](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#std-label-log-messages-ref), in the `attr.command.cursor.comment` field.; [Database profiler](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md#std-label-profiler) output, in the [`command.comment`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md#mongodb-data-system.profile.command) field.; [`currentOp`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/currentop.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.currentOp) output, in the [`command.comment`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/currentop.md#mongodb-data-currentOp.command) field. Set `fullDocument` to `"updateLookup"` to direct [`watch()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.watch.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.watch) to look up the most current majority-committed version of the updated document. [`watch()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.watch.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.watch) returns a `fullDocument` field with the document lookup in addition to the `updateDescription` delta. Starting in MongoDB 6.0, you can set `fullDocument` to: `"whenAvailable"` to output the document post-image, if available, after the document was inserted, replaced, or updated.; `"required"` to output the document post-image after the document was inserted, replaced, or updated. Raises an error if the post-image is not available. | | `fullDocumentBeforeChange` | string | Optional. Starting in MongoDB 6.0, you can use the new `fullDocumentBeforeChange` field and set it to: `"whenAvailable"` to output the document pre-image, if available, before the document was replaced, updated, or deleted.; `"required"` to output the document pre-image before the document was replaced, updated, or deleted. Raises an error if the pre-image is not available.; `"off"` to suppress the document pre-image. `"off"` is the default. | | `batchSize` | int | Optional. The maximum number of documents that can be returned in each batch of a change stream. By default, [`watch()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.watch.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.watch) has an initial batch size of the lesser of `101` documents or 16 mebibytes (MiB) worth of documents. Subsequent batches have a maximum size of 16 mebibytes.This option can enforce a smaller limit than 16 MiB, but not a larger one. When set, the `batchSize` is the lesser of `batchSize` documents or 16 MiB worth of documents. Has the same functionality as [`cursor.batchSize()`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.batchsize.md#mongodb-method-cursor.batchSize) | | `maxAwaitTimeMS` | int | Optional. The maximum amount of time in milliseconds the server waits for new data changes to report to the change stream cursor before returning an empty batch. Defaults to `1000` milliseconds. | | `collation` | document | Optional. Pass a [collation document](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation-document-fields) to specify a collation for the change stream cursor. Defaults to `simple` binary comparison if omitted. | | `showExpandedEvents` | boolean | Optional. Starting in MongoDB 6.0, change streams support change notifications for DDL events, like the [createIndexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/change-events/createindexes.md#std-label-change-event-createIndexes) and [dropIndexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/change-events/dropindexes.md#std-label-change-event-dropIndexes) events. To include expanded events in a change stream, create the change stream cursor using the `showExpandedEvents` option. **New in version 6.0** | | `startAtOperationTime` | Timestamp | Optional. The starting point for the change stream. If the specified starting point is in the past, it must be in the time range of the oplog. To check the time range of the oplog, see [`rs.printReplicationInfo()`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/rs.printreplicationinfo.md#mongodb-method-rs.printReplicationInfo) `startAtOperationTime` is mutually exclusive with `resumeAfter` and `startAfter`. | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.watch.md#fields · keywords: cursor, resumeAfter, watch(), _id, startAfter, startAtOperationTime

- [statement] Mitigations named by the Netdata guide: put the shard key or leading prefix in predicates, set maxTimeMS on unavoidable scatter-gather queries, avoid deep skip() pagination, and re-evaluate the shard key against dominant query shapes. A low-cardinality key (e.g. continent, at most seven chunks) limits scaling regardless of shard count. - [fact] A compound index supports a sort on all its keys or on a prefix, with sort keys in index order. Directions must match the index pattern or its exact inverse: {a:1,b:-1} supports {a:1,b:-1} and {a:-1,b:1}, but not {a:1,b:1} or {a:-1,b:-1}. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sort-results-with-indexes/ · keywords: blocking sort, index, Blocking Sort and Index-Backed Sort
- [fact] An index can serve a sort on a non-prefix subset of its keys only if the query has equality conditions on all index keys that precede the sort keys. With index {a,b,c,d}, find({a:{$gt:2}}).sort({c:1}) does not use the index efficiently. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sort-results-with-indexes/ · keywords: blocking sort, index, Blocking Sort and Index-Backed Sort
- [fact] ESR guideline: put equality keys first, then sort keys, then range keys, so the index delivers sorted output without an in-memory sort. Sorting after equality also makes the sort non-blocking. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline/ · keywords: blocking sort, index, Blocking Sort and Index-Backed Sort
- [fact] countDocuments() rejects $where, $near and $nearSphere in its query; the documented substitutes are $expr and $geoWithin with $center / $centerSphere. Inside a transaction, both countDocuments() and estimatedDocumentCount() do not filter out uncommitted multi-document transactions. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.countDocuments/ · keywords: count, query operator anti-pattern, Count and Distinct and Sampling Optimization
- [fact] Hashed sharding gives more even distribution at the cost of targeting. Post-hash, documents with close key values are unlikely to share a shard, so mongos is more likely to broadcast a ranged query. Equality matches can still be targeted to a single shard. The docs say 'more likely', not 'always'. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/hashed-sharding/ · keywords: query operator anti-pattern, sharded query targeting, Sharded Query Targeting and Scatter-Gather
- [passage] Queries that include a sort by [`$natural`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.hint.md#mongodb-operator-metaOp.-natural) order do **not** use indexes to fulfill the query predicate with the following exception: If the query predicate is an equality condition on the `_id` field `{ _id: <value> }`, then the query with the sort by [`$natural`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.hint.md#mongodb-operator-metaOp.-natural) order can use the `_id` index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.sort.md#index-use · keywords: cursor, index, query shape, $natural, _id, { _id: <value> }
- [passage] An aggregation pipeline can use [indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/indexes.md#std-label-indexes) from the input collection to improve performance. Using an index limits the amount of documents a stage processes. Ideally, an index can [cover](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-optimization.md#std-label-read-operations-covered-query) the stage query. A covered query has especially high performance, since the index returns all matching documents. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-optimization.md#indexes · keywords: index, projection, query optimization

- [fact] batchSize changes only how many documents each network round trip fetches. Driver iteration (next, hasNext, for-await) still yields one document at a time from the fetched batch. With batchSize 1 and 1000 results the driver issues 999 getMore calls. — https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/mis-understanding-batchsize/169713/2 · keywords: cursor, read preference, Cursor and Read-Path Tuning (batchSize and maxTimeMS and read preference)
- [fact] Too large a batchSize makes the cursor allocate more resources than needed; too small adds network round trips. A batchSize of 0 opens the cursor and returns no documents in the first batch. Third-party sizing ranges (50-200 for large documents or memory limits, 500-2000 for small documents and bulk throughput) are heuristics, not vendor guidance. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.batchSize.md · keywords: cursor, read preference, Cursor and Read-Path Tuning (batchSize and maxTimeMS and read preference)
- [fact] Server sessions idle for 30 minutes expire and the server may kill their cursors, including cursors with noCursorTimeout or a maxTimeMS over 30 minutes. A very large maxTimeMS therefore does not keep a cursor alive. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.maxTimeMS.md · keywords: cursor, read preference, Cursor and Read-Path Tuning (batchSize and maxTimeMS and read preference)
- [statement] From MongoDB 8.2, long-running secondary reads in a sharded cluster can be terminated before orphaned-document cleanup after a chunk migration; the terminateSecondaryReadsOnOrphanCleanup parameter controls this. Long scans on secondaries should expect and retry this. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/read-preference.md · keywords: cursor, read preference, Cursor and Read-Path Tuning (batchSize and maxTimeMS and read preference)
- [statement] Historic bug: in MongoDB 3.0.0-3.0.3, long-running secondary reads did not yield and could stall replication, growing lag and stale reads (SERVER-18190, fixed in 3.0.4). Heavy secondary reads still compete with oplog application for resources. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-18190 · keywords: cursor, read preference, Cursor and Read-Path Tuning (batchSize and maxTimeMS and read preference)

- [fact] MongoDB's documented range-query pagination: pick a field such as _id that changes consistently over time and has a unique index, filter with $lt (descending) or $gt (ascending), sort on it, and store the last-seen value for the next query. Range queries use indexes to avoid scanning unwanted documents. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.2/reference/method/cursor.skip/ · keywords: index, pagination, Pagination Patterns (skip-limit vs range-keyset)
- [fact] For a non-unique sort field such as createdAt, keyset pagination needs a compound filter: $or of {createdAt < last} and {createdAt == last, _id < lastId}, sorted by {createdAt:-1,_id:-1}, backed by an index with the same fields and directions. — https://blog.openreplay.com/pagination-patterns-mongodb/ · keywords: index, pagination, Pagination Patterns (skip-limit vs range-keyset)

- [passage] | Field Name | Description | | --- | --- | | `latency` | The total latency, in microseconds. | | `ops` | The total number of operations performed on the collection since startup. | | `histogram` | An array of embedded documents, each representing a latency range. Each document covers twice the previous document's range. For lower values between 2048 microseconds and roughly 1 second, the histogram includes half-steps. This field only exists given the `latencyStats: { histograms: true }` option. Empty ranges with a zero `count` are omitted from the output. Each document has the following fields: `micros`: the inclusive lower bound of the current latency range, in microseconds.The document's range spans between the previous document's `micros` value, exclusive, and this document's `micros` value, inclusive.; `count`: the number of operations with latency less than or equal to `micros`. For example, if `collStats` returns the following histogram: `histogram: [ { micros: Long(0), count: Long(10) }, { micros: Long(2), count: Long(1) }, { micros: Long(4096), count: Long(1) }, { micros: Long(16384), count: Long(1000) }, { micros: Long(49152), count: Long(100) } ]` This indicates that there were : 10 operations taking 2 microsecond or less; 1 operation in the range [2, 4) microseconds; 1 operation in the range [4096, 6144) microseconds; 1000 operations in the range [16384, 24576) microseconds; 100 operations in the range [49152, 65536) microseconds | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/collStats.md#latencystats-document · keywords: count, latency, ops, histogram, latencyStats: { histograms: true }, micros
